title: Distributions: Ubuntu/Debian, RHEL, Rocky, Alma and SUSE

videos.script: One kernel. Roughly a hundred distributions built on it, and every one of them is Linux. {{many}} So people ask which is best, and that is the wrong question — the right one is what actually differs, because the honest answer is: less than you fear, and in places you would not guess. {{differs}} Here is when it matters. It is three in the morning, something is down, and you have a shell on a machine you did not set up. The command you were about to type does not exist there. The service has a different name. The configuration is in a different file. {{night}} Everything in this lesson exists to make that moment boring. By the end of it you will know the four or five families, what a distribution actually bundles, and the one command to run before anything else when you arrive somewhere new. {{title}}

Three situations, three different answers, and none of them is a favourite. {{open}} First: a company web server, going into production, maintained by people who are not you. You want a long support window and boring updates. That is a long-term release from a big family — Ubuntu LTS, or Rocky or Alma if the software you are running publishes for Red Hat. Ten years of security updates and no surprises. {{server}} Second: a container image for a small service. Now you want the opposite — the smallest thing that runs your program, because every megabyte is shipped a thousand times. Alpine, if your program is happy with musl. Debian slim if it is not, and I will show you in a moment how to tell. {{container}} Third: your own laptop, for learning. Here the answer is whatever the documentation you are about to read assumes — which in practice means Ubuntu, because that is what the tutorials were written against. Fighting that is a tax you pay for no benefit while you are learning. {{laptop}} Notice what did not decide any of those: which one is technically best. Support window, size, and what the ecosystem expects. That is the whole of it. {{summary}}

So: you do not have to choose. {{open}} That is the thing to carry out of this lesson. Somebody else chose, for the machine you are about to be handed, and your job is to find out what they chose and behave accordingly. {{chosen}} Which is one command. Cat, etc, os-release. ID tells you the distribution, ID underscore LIKE tells you the family — and the family is what decides your package manager, your service names and half your paths. {{command}} Make it a reflex. Arrive, check, then type. It costs two seconds and it is the difference between apt install on a machine that has never heard of apt, and the right command the first time. {{reflex}} Next lesson leaves this behind entirely. The filesystem — the tree, absolute and relative paths, and the commands you will use more than all the others put together. It is the longest lesson in the course and the one everything after it stands on. {{next}} Drill first.
